design_detail: National register-based adoption study (Archives of General Psychiatry 2012; read as the NIH author manuscript). 18,115 Swedish adoptees born 1950–1993 who first lived with their adoptive parents by age 10 (12,783 by age 5), linked through personal identity numbers to 78,079 biological parents and siblings they were not raised with and 51,208 adoptive parents and siblings they were raised with, in 9 national registers covering 1961–2009. The outcome is the study's register-defined 'drug abuse' (DA): drug-use-disorder or drug-psychosis diagnoses (alcohol and tobacco excluded) in hospital, outpatient, primary-care and death records, convictions under two crime-register codes for crimes related to drug abuse (convictions only for alcohol-related crimes, or for drug trafficking or possession, excluded), or long-term high-volume collection of prescribed sedatives, hypnotics or opioids. Analyses: DA rates in relatives of adoptees and parents with and without DA; a 'genetic' risk index built from biological relatives and an 'environmental' risk index built from the adoptive family (each the predicted probability from a logistic regression in the same sample, cut into deciles); and a gene × environment interaction on the scale of raw probabilities. No heritability percentage is estimated.
can_establish: That in Swedish adoptees born 1950–1993 with register information on a biological parent, a DA record was more common when biological parents or siblings they were not raised with had DA, alcohol problems, psychiatric hospitalization or convictions, and also when the adoptive home included an adoptive sibling with DA or was disrupted by divorce or a parent's death; that is, factors passed on from biological relatives and factors of the rearing home both predict DA, which a design in intact families cannot separate.
cannot_establish: A heritability percentage (none is estimated); that the biological-relative association is purely genetic (prenatal exposure, care before placement and selective placement are reduced but not excluded); that the gene × environment interaction holds on a multiplicative (odds) scale, which was not reported; or that the figures apply outside Swedish adoptions of the 1950s to 1990s with a biological parent in the registers, or outside its register definition of drug abuse.

sample.recruitment: Registry: all people born 1950–1993 who had been adopted, with information on both adoptive parents and at least one biological parent, from the Multi-Generation Register (the paper does not say 'born in Sweden'; requiring register information on a biological parent in practice limits the sample to children whose biological parents were in the Swedish registers), linked to the hospital discharge (1964–2009), prescribed drug (2005–2009), mortality (1961–2009), outpatient (2001–2009), primary health care (2001–2007, Stockholm and middle Sweden only), crime (1973–2007) registers and censuses (Methods; Sample).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: adoptions by biological relatives or by an adoptive parent living with a biological parent; biological siblings reared with the adoptee. Age at first cohabitation with adoptive parents (AFCAP), estimated from 5-yearly censuses and therefore an upper bound, at most 10 years (main cohort) or 5 years (sensitivity cohort) (Sample).
sample.demographics: Adoptees 52.2% male; mean (SD) age at last available information 46.2 (8.5) years; mean AFCAP 4.4 years (Results › General description; Table 2). Biological parents had more DA (5.8% vs 1.0%), psychiatric hospitalization (18.8% vs 3.1%), alcoholism hospitalization (15.9% vs 0.9%), convictions (41.3% vs 9.4%), low education (76.5% vs 42.8%) and maternal divorce (38.7% vs 6.8%) than adoptive parents (Table 2).
sample.attrition: Not applicable as such (register follow-up). Emigration, death and the different years each register covers are not handled as time at risk; logistic regression treats DA as ever or never.
sample.selection_effects: Only adoptions with register information on a biological parent (in practice, children whose biological parents were in the Swedish registers; the paper does not say 'domestic adoptions'); adoptive families were selected for placement and carry little risk (1.0% DA in adoptive parents), so the range of adoptive-home environments is narrow. Selective placement was modest (the two risk indices correlated +0.11; a +0.14 educational correlation between biological and adoptive parents in earlier Swedish work). At least 70.9% lived with their adoptive parents by age 5 (an estimate from 5-yearly censuses), so up to about 3 in 10 may have been placed later; the authors say children were usually removed from their mothers shortly after birth and spent the time before placement in nursery or foster homes (Methodological limitations, 2nd–3rd paragraphs).

exposure.measurement: Register records of relatives: DA (same definition as the outcome), hospitalization for alcoholism (ICD-8 291, 303; ICD-9 291, 303; ICD-10 F10) or psychiatric illness, any criminal conviction, education (low or high, by the 75th percentile within birth decade), divorce, death, medical hospitalization, maternal age. Adoptive-family variables were counted from first cohabitation until the adoptee was 20; biological-relative and adoptive-sibling variables over their whole lives (Genetic risk score; Environmental risk score).
exposure.polysubstance: DA covers all drugs other than alcohol and tobacco together (ICD-10 F11–F16, F18–F19 and their ICD-8 and ICD-9 equivalents); no results by drug.

comparison.controls: Adoptees whose biological (or adoptive) relatives had no DA record; relatives of adoptees without DA.
comparison.matching: None; birth year controlled in all analyses after the description; sex and AFCAP in the risk-index models.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Mothers' substance use during pregnancy, the care adoptees received before placement, and the criteria by which agencies matched children to adoptive homes were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Register-defined DA: ICD-8 304; ICD-9 292 and 304; ICD-10 F10–F19 except F10 and F17, in hospital discharge, mortality, outpatient and primary-care registers; convictions under crime codes 5011 and 5012 (crimes related only to alcohol, or to drug trafficking or possession, excluded); or collection of prescribed hypnotics and sedatives (ATC N05C, N05BA) or opioids (N02A) averaging more than 4 daily doses over 12 months, cancer patients excluded (Outcome variable).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation against interviews. The 820 adoptee cases came from discharge (527), crime (313), outpatient (264), prescribed drug (118) and primary care (8) registers, with overlap; between-register odds ratios of registration ranged from 5.6 (prescription vs crime) to 118.0 (discharge vs outpatient) (Table 1). The authors compare Sweden's register prevalence with a Norwegian survey's 3.4% lifetime DSM-III-R abuse or dependence (Methodological limitations, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Ever having a DA record in any of the registers up to 2009; the authors say the construct may be broader than DSM-IV dependence and can include false negatives (no contact with services) and false positives (arrest or treatment without a use disorder; high-dose opioids for chronic pain).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (one outcome; many predictors, selected for the risk indices at P<.10).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Register entries were made independently of the study and of relatives' records.

analysis.effect_sizes: DA in adoptees 4.5% (95% CI 4.2–4.8) vs 2.9% in all Sweden for the same birth years. Adoptees of biological parents with vs without DA 8.6% vs 4.2%, OR 2.09 (1.66–2.62), χ²(1)=39.4; none, one or both biological parents with DA 4.2%, 8.2%, 11.9%, χ²(2)=44.0; biological father 9.9%, mother 8.2%. Biological full siblings 10.7% vs 6.1%, OR 1.84 (1.28–2.64); half siblings 7.4% vs 5.3%, OR 1.41 (1.19–1.67); adoptive parents 6.8% vs 4.5%, OR 1.55 (0.86–2.80), P=.15; adoptive siblings 6.2% vs 3.2%, OR 1.95 (1.43–2.65) (Results; Table 3; χ² values read from the page's MathJax source). Risk indices, OR per decile: genetic 1.13 (1.10–1.16), environmental 1.10 (1.07–1.12); jointly with sex, AFCAP and birth year 1.12 (1.09–1.15) and 1.09 (1.06–1.12); male sex 1.44 (1.24–1.66) (Table 5). Probability scale (Table 6): genetic 0.0049 and environmental 0.0036 per decile, male +0.0151; with the interaction, genetic 0.0028, environmental 0.0015 (−0.0006 to 0.0036), interaction 0.0005 (0.0001–0.0008), P<.05. Editors' calculation from Table 6: each environmental decile adds about 0.15 percentage points of risk at the lowest genetic decile and about 0.6 points at the highest (0.0015 + 9×0.0005).
analysis.covariates: Birth year (after the descriptive analyses); sex and AFCAP in the risk-index models. The relative-pair odds ratios do not say what they were adjusted for or how several siblings of one adoptee were handled.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The gene × environment test and its probability scale are described as an a priori aim (Statistical analysis); no protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: The sensitivity analysis in adoptees placed by age 5 (n=12,783) is reported only as an unchanged broad pattern, without numbers; the interaction on the logistic scale is not reported; the risk indices were built and tested in the same sample, with predictors chosen at P<.10.
analysis.power: Not reported; large cohort, but only about 1% of adoptive parents had DA, so the adoptive-parent comparison is imprecise (OR 1.55, 0.86–2.80).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Moderate familial associations in both directions of the adoption design: odds ratios of about 1.4 to 2.1 for DA in biological relatives not reared together, and about 2 for adoptive siblings reared together; a non-significant, imprecise association with adoptive parents' DA; data-derived risk indices from the biological and adoptive families each predicting DA; and a positive interaction between them on the scale of absolute risk.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that DA is strongly influenced by genetic risk factors and that adverse environments are more pathogenic in people at high genetic risk; the Comment calls the result a replication of the strong genetic contribution found in twin studies (1st paragraph). No heritability was estimated, and the genetic index includes biological parents' education and divorce, so it captures whatever passes from biological parents (genes, prenatal environment, care before placement, selective placement), not genes alone. The authors say they could "rule out" intrauterine effects because risk was greater with affected fathers than mothers (Comment, 3rd paragraph), but the rates were 9.9% and 8.2% with overlapping intervals (7.2–12.1 and 6.3–10.5) and no test of the difference is reported. The conclusion that social influences shared with adoptive siblings are more potent than transmission from adoptive parents (Comment, 5th paragraph) compares a significant with a non-significant result; the adoptive-parent interval (0.86–2.80) contains the sibling estimate, and only 1.0% of adoptive parents had DA. The interaction holds on the probability scale chosen a priori; the paper does not show whether it holds on the odds scale, where two risk factors that multiply each other's odds produce an interaction of this kind on the probability scale.

timeline.event: US adoption studies of 197 adoptees whose parents were selected from hospital and prison records for alcohol problems, drug use or antisocial behaviour (Cadoret et al., 1995, 1996, as described in this paper): consistent with a genetic contribution.

Twin study of DSM-III-R drug abuse and dependence in 3,372 male twin pairs (Tsuang et al., 1996, as cited): one of four population twin studies from Australia and the US that the authors say they replicate.
Heritability in the genomics era: what a heritability figure does and does not mean (Visscher et al., 2008); not yet appraised

246 adoptive adolescent same-sex sibling pairs resembled each other for substance use disorders (Buchanan et al., 2009, as described in this paper): consistent with the shared-environment finding, which some adult twin studies did not show.
Narrative review of the genetic epidemiology of substance use disorders, without heritability estimates; appraised in this batch

replication.where_it_stands: The association with biological relatives not reared together agrees with the earlier twin and adoption studies the authors cite; the substantial association with adoptive siblings, read as shared environment, differs from some adult twin studies that found little shared environment for lifetime drug use disorders (Comment, 5th paragraph). Later Swedish register work by the same group was not read in this round.

funding.funder: Grant RO1 DA030005 from the National Institute of Drug Abuse; grants 2008-3110 and 2008-2638 from the Swedish Research Council; a project grant from ALF, Lund, Sweden. The sponsors had no role in design, conduct, analysis, interpretation or the manuscript (Acknowledgments › Funding/Support; Role of the Sponsors).
funding.affiliations_note: Virginia Institute for Psychiatric and Behavioral Genetics, Virginia Commonwealth University; Center for Primary Health Care Research, Lund University; Stanford Prevention Research Center. The interaction scale follows the first author's earlier methods paper (Kendler & Gardner, 2010, as cited). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Adoption and twin designs analysed together in the same register population with drug-specific, validated outcomes, time-to-event models that account for register coverage, emigration and death, risk indices built in one half of the data and tested in the other, the gene × environment interaction reported on both the probability and odds scales, and direct data on prenatal exposure and age at placement; ideally repeated in another country and in later birth cohorts.

domains.note: The adoption design removes genetic confounding of rearing-environment effects and rearing confounding of biological-relative effects, but prenatal exposure, care before placement (up to about 3 in 10 possibly placed after age 5) and selective placement remain; the father-versus-mother argument against prenatal effects is not tested.

Relatives' DA, psychiatric and criminal histories come from registers with different coverage periods, so older relatives and earlier decades are measured differently; misclassification is probably non-differential.

National register of adoptions with near-complete identity linkage; the requirement of information on at least one biological parent (which in practice limits the sample to children whose biological parents were in the Swedish registers) limits generality more than it biases the associations.

Outpatient, prescription and primary-care registers cover only 2001–2009 (primary care only Stockholm and middle Sweden), so ascertainment differs by birth cohort; emigration and death are not handled; missing biological fathers are not described.

Broad register construct mixing diagnoses, convictions for crimes the register codes as related to drug abuse (codes 5011 and 5012; alcohol-only, trafficking and possession convictions excluded) and long-term high-volume prescriptions, not validated against interviews; families with criminal or psychiatric records may also be more visible to police and services.
Risk indices built and tested in the same data with predictors chosen at P<.10; the age-5 sensitivity analysis reported without numbers; the odds-scale interaction not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For the familial associations (biological relatives not reared together; adoptive siblings reared together) the national adoption design is strong and the outcome, though broad, is recorded independently of the study, so the main concerns are residual prenatal and pre-placement effects, a heterogeneous register outcome and cohort-dependent ascertainment. The risk-index and gene × environment results are weaker: data-derived indices, no validation and a scale-dependent interaction. The study may be cited for odds ratios of DA in biological and adoptive relatives of Swedish adoptees born 1950–1993, with the register definition stated; it may not be cited for a heritability percentage, for a purely genetic interpretation of the biological-relative association, or for gene × environment interaction without naming the probability scale.

key_findings.finding: Cohort: 18,115 Swedish adoptees born 1950–1993 who first lived with their adoptive parents by age 10 (12,783 by age 5), with 78,079 biological parents and siblings and 51,208 adoptive parents and siblings; adoptees 52.2% male, mean (SD) age at last information 46.2 (8.5) years, mean age at first cohabitation with adoptive parents 4.4 years; follow-up in registers 1961–2009.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Sample; Results › General description, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: DA, as defined from registers, was recorded in 4.5% (95% CI 4.2–4.8) of adoptees (820 people) against 2.9% in all of Sweden for the same birth years; the 820 cases came from hospital discharge (527), crime (313), outpatient (264), prescribed drug (118) and primary care (8) registers, with overlap.
key_findings.locator: Results › General description, 1st paragraph; Methods › Outcome variable, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Among adoptees, DA rose across birth decades (1950–59 to 1980–93: 4.1%, 4.6%, 5.0%, 6.5%) while the national rate stayed between 2.8% and 3.1% with no trend; birth year was controlled in later analyses.

Adopted-away children of biological parents with DA had DA in 8.6% vs 4.2% when neither biological parent had DA (OR 2.09, 95% CI 1.66–2.62; χ²(1)=39.4, P<.001); with none, one or both biological parents affected, 4.2%, 8.2% and 11.9% (χ²(2)=44.0, P<.001); with an affected biological father 9.9% (7.2–12.1), mother 8.2% (6.3–10.5).
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug abuse in biological and adoptive relatives, 1st paragraph; Table 3
key_findings.note: χ² values are inline MathJax on the PMC page and were read from its math source.

key_findings.finding: Biological siblings not reared with the adoptee: full siblings of adoptees with DA had DA in 10.7% vs 6.1% (OR 1.84, 1.28–2.64); half siblings 7.4% vs 5.3% (OR 1.41, 1.19–1.67).
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug abuse in biological and adoptive relatives, 1st paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Rearing family: adoptees raised by an adoptive parent with DA had DA in 6.8% vs 4.5% (OR 1.55, 0.86–2.80, P=.15; only 1.0% of adoptive parents had DA); genetically unrelated adoptive siblings of adoptees with DA had DA in 6.2% vs 3.2% (OR 1.95, 1.43–2.65, P<.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug abuse in biological and adoptive relatives, 2nd paragraph; Tables 2 and 3

key_findings.finding: Risk indices (deciles of predicted probability): 'genetic' index from biological parents and siblings (DA, alcoholism, psychiatric hospitalization, convictions, low education, divorce, maternal age) OR 1.13 per decile (1.10–1.16); 'environmental' index from the adoptive family (parental divorce, death, alcoholism, convictions, medical hospitalization, maternal age; adoptive siblings' DA and hospitalizations) OR 1.10 (1.07–1.12); jointly 1.12 and 1.09; male sex OR 1.44 (1.24–1.66); the two indices correlated +0.11.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictors of genetic and environmental risk, 1st–3rd paragraphs; Tables 4 and 5
key_findings.note: The authors' lowest-to-highest decile odds ratios (3.39 and 2.59) use ten steps; with deciles coded 0 to 9 the contrast is 1.13^9≈3.0 and 1.10^9≈2.4 (editors' calculation; see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: In the multivariable models that built the indices, DA in adoptees was predicted by biological parents' DA (OR 1.44, 1.11–1.85), alcoholism (1.36), psychiatric hospitalization (1.26) and convictions (1.22), and by adoptive siblings' DA (1.76, 1.16–2.67), the adoptive mother's divorce (1.31, 1.03–1.68) and an adoptive parent's death (1.37, 1.08–1.73); biological siblings' DA added nothing once parents were in the model (1.02, 0.60–1.72).

Gene × environment on the probability scale: interaction coefficient 0.0005 per decile × decile (95% CI 0.0001–0.0008, P<.05); with it, the environmental main effect fell to 0.0015 (−0.0006 to 0.0036). Each environmental decile thus added about 0.15 percentage points of risk at the lowest genetic decile and about 0.6 at the highest (editors' calculation).
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictors of genetic and environmental risk, 5th paragraph; Table 6; Figure
key_findings.note: Scale-dependent: the paper does not report the interaction on the odds scale.

key_findings.finding: Sex: modest evidence that males were more sensitive to genetic risk (sex × genetic index P=.03); no sex difference in sensitivity to the environmental index (P=.91).
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictors of genetic and environmental risk, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Checks for contact before placement: age at first cohabitation was negatively, not positively, associated with DA (univariate OR 0.96 per year, 0.93–0.98; 1.00 when adjusted); it did not interact with the environmental index (P=.88); at least 70.9% lived with adoptive parents by age 5; results in the age-5 cohort were described as broadly unchanged, without numbers.

The authors' limitations: register case-finding gives false negatives (people never in contact with services) and false positives (arrest or treatment without a use disorder; high-dose opioids for chronic pain), the construct may be broader than DSM-IV dependence, and selective placement was modest.

reporting_issues.issue: The odds ratios between the lowest and highest deciles of the risk indices are computed as 1.13^10=3.39 and 1.10^10=2.59, but the deciles are coded 0 to 9 (Figure legend), so there are nine steps: 1.13^9≈3.0 and 1.10^9≈2.4 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript): Results › Predictors of genetic and environmental risk, 2nd paragraph; Figure legend
reporting_issues.consequence: The extreme-decile contrasts are overstated by one decile step (about 13% and 10%).

reporting_issues.issue: The national prevalence of DA for the same birth years is 2.9% in the Results (with decade values of 2.8% to 3.1%) but 2.7% in the Methodological limitations, where it is compared with Norway's 3.4%.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript): Results › General description, 1st–2nd paragraphs; Methodological limitations, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the comparison with the Norwegian survey uses a figure that does not match the Results.

reporting_issues.issue: For half siblings and adoptive siblings the printed χ²(1) values (9.7 and 13.9) are smaller than those implied by the printed odds ratios and intervals (about 15.8 and 18.0, editors' calculation from the log-odds-ratio standard error), while for biological parents, full siblings and adoptive parents they agree; χ²(1)=9.7 also corresponds to P≈.002, not the printed P=.001. The paper does not say how several siblings of the same adoptee (43,537 half siblings for 14,884 adoptees) were handled.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript): Results › Drug abuse in biological and adoptive relatives, 1st–2nd paragraphs; Tables 2 and 3
reporting_issues.consequence: The precision of the sibling odds ratios is uncertain; if siblings of one adoptee were counted as independent pairs, the intervals are too narrow.

reporting_issues.issue: The biological fathers' rate of 9.9% lies off-centre in its interval (7.2–12.1; midpoint 9.65), unlike the other rows of Table 3, whose intervals are skewed upward as expected for proportions.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript): Table 3, row Biological father; Results, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: A misprint of the estimate or a limit is possible; this row is the basis of the authors' argument against intrauterine effects.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's odds ratios of registration between registers have very narrow intervals (for example 118.0, 115.7–120.4) that cannot come from the cohort's 820 cases; the population used for Table 1 is not stated.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript): Methods › Outcome variable, 4th paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 1 probably describes agreement between registers in a larger population; overlap among the adoptees' cases is given only as counts per register.

reporting_issues.issue: The sex interactions were added to the model said to be depicted in Table 4, but the joint model with sex, AFCAP and birth year is in Table 5; Table 4's column heading reads 'Adaptive Relations'.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript): Results › Predictors, 4th paragraph; Tables 4 and 5

reporting_issues.issue: Two small inconsistencies: Table 4 prints the biological parents' univariate odds ratio as 2.09 (1.66–2.63), while the abstract and Results give 2.09 (1.66–2.62); and the authors write that at least 70.9% of adoptees lived with their adoptive parents by age 5, while the age-5 cohort is 12,783 of 18,115, that is 70.6% (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript): Table 4, Parents › Drug abuse row, Biological Relations univariate column; Abstract › Results; Results › Drug abuse in biological and adoptive relatives, 1st paragraph; Sample; Methodological limitations, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor rounding or copying slips that change no conclusion; 'up to about 3 in 10 placed after age 5' holds with either figure.
